To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the left ventricle of people with type 1 diabetes has a blunted contractile response to exercise that is not explained by the presence of microvascular disease, and the left ventricles of people with type 2 diabetes have a blunted contractility and impaired diastolic function at rest and exercise that are associated with the presence of microangiopathy.
the diabetic heart is less efficient at pumping blood during exercise, and this is likely caused by the accumulation of fat and fibrous tissue within the heart.

1) exercise training does not improve left ventricular systolic and diastolic function in people with type II diabetes; 2) exercise training does improve left ventricular diastolic function and exercise capacity in people with type I diabetes; and 3) people with type II diabetic cardiomyopathy are unable to achieve a similar improvement in left ventricular dias-tolic function as people with type I diabetic cardiomyopathy
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the heart in exercise intolerance and the challenge to find effective exercise interventions for the type 2 diabetic heart.
the effects of exercise on cardiac function in type 2 diabetes, and how these effects can be enhanced by exercise prescription and exercise training.

the development of novel exercise training interventions for people with type-2 diabetes, with the aim of improving exercise capacity, left ventricular function (including diastolic dysfunction) and cardiovascular disease risk.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the heart in type 2 diabetes is abnormal, and that exercise interventions are needed to improve the function and reserve of the diabetic heart.
exercise training in people with type II diabetes is beneficial, but that the optimal intensity and duration of exercise training has not been determined.
the diabetic heart is less efficient at rest and during exercise, and that the mechanisms responsible for these changes are complex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the left ventricle of the diabetic heart is a key determinant of exercise capacity.
the diabetic heart has a reduced ability to increase cardiac output and oxygen delivery to the exercising skeletal muscle, and that this may be a major contributor to exercise intolerance.
the diabetic heart is not a healthy heart and that exercise training is a powerful intervention to improve cardiac function and reduce the risk of heart disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the left ventricle of the diabetic heart is a significant barrier to exercise tolerance, which may limit the benefits of exercise in people with diabetes.
people with type 1 diabetes have normal resting cardiac function, but reduced cardiac reserve, which limits the amount of exercise they can do without causing heart failure.
the diabetic heart is not normal and that it is not normal in the resting state or during exercise.
